title: Enigma
full_review:
A code-breaking genius takes another crack at deciphering German code in the reasonably entertaining historical thriller "Enigma" (Manhattan Pictures).

Set in 1943 England, the film is layered with several story strands. It is as much a tale about obsession, love and betrayal as it is about beating the Nazis by breaking down their nearly impenetrable secret code. But it is in this act of layering that the film falters, unable to satisfactorily pull everything together. Directed by Michael Apted from a screenplay adapted by Tom Stoppard from Robert Harris' bestseller, "Enigma" nonetheless pleases with dynamic editing of story lines as well as its heady atmospherics.

The title makes reference not only to the Nazis' "Enigma machine" but also to the lanky blonde bombshell Claire Romilly (Saffron Burrows, looking rail thin), who has driven code-breaking genius Tom Jericho (Dougray Scott) beyond distraction into a nervous breakdown. Brought back from his "resting place" to help the top-secret intelligence operation at Bletchley Park, Jericho suspects that the missing Claire might also be a traitor. But first on his plate is to break the new code the Germans have formulated before a United States convoy of supply ships is attacked by encircling Nazi submarines.

Claire's whereabouts are a constant distraction to Jericho, and he enlists the help of Claire's roommate Hester (Kate Winslet, successfully looking frumpy) to find her. At this point the film loads up the subplots, beginning with the mystery of a mass grave somewhere on the Eastern front where Germans are broadcasting secret messages. The mystery of Claire's disappearance, and where her loyalties lie, thickens. And looming in the background is the time constraints faced by the crossword puzzlers at Bletchley Park who are attempting to unravel the strange sequence of letters and win the war. Periodically smarmy spy extraordinaire Wigram (Jeremy Northam) pops in to harass Jericho or to offer the audience another piece of information that will eventually fit into the "Enigma" puzzle.

The film's successes lie in crosscutting between the story lines, piquing the viewer's interest and leading on the audience. But the ending is a let down, not quite measuring up to the preceding material. Fine performances compensate to a certain extent, particularly Northam, who makes excellent use of his dry wit and deadpan delivery.

The American film "U-571" stoked up considerable annoyance among British historians because it credited Americans with breaking the Nazi code. And "Enigma" has come under the same scrutiny as patriotic Poles have insisted that it was their countrymen, not the Brits, who captured the Enigma machine. Without dismissing the controversy, "Enigma" is diverting fare despite its shortcomings.

Due to a brief sexual encounter with partial nudity and minimal rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
